title: One step up the earthquake magnitude scale means about 32 times more energy
body: On 9 October 2026 a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck near Pitaloza Arriba, Panama, according to the [USGS](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/eventpage/us6000u18k); the first estimate, from the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center, had been 8.0. Magnitude measures a quake's moment: the stiffness of the rock times the area of fault that slipped times how far it slipped. The scale counts in powers of ten, so each whole step means waves about 10 times taller on a seismogram and about 32 times more energy ([USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/programs/earthquake-hazards/earthquake-magnitude-energy-release-and-shaking-intensity)). Two steps is about 1,000 times, and 8.0 would have meant almost three times the energy of 7.7. This quake was left-lateral strike-slip, the two sides of the fault sliding past each other sideways, on the small plate Panama sits on, squeezed between the Cocos, Nazca, Caribbean and South American plates.

slides.question: An earthquake one whole step higher on the magnitude scale releases about how many times more energy?
slides.explanation: About 32 times (10 to the power 1.5 is 31.6), according to the US Geological Survey, while the waves on a seismogram swing about 10 times higher.

slides.alt: Animation on seismograph paper: a trace swings wide and reads 7.7, first estimated at 8.0. Moment is rigidity × area × slip; a road across a locked fault bends, then snaps sideways. Squares count the energy: 32 times per step, 1,000 for two. Then Panama's plates and earlier quakes.

slides.prompt: Set a fault's length, depth and slip. Can you build a magnitude 7.7, like the quake in Panama on 9 October 2026?
slides.takeaway: A big fault: 100 km long and 20 km deep, slipping 6.4 m, makes a 7.7. Doubling the slip adds only 0.2; a whole step needs 32 times the area × slip.

slides.heading: Panama, 9 Oct 2026: energy in units of the 6.6 quake that followed the 7.7
slides.note: Computed with the US Geological Survey's rule of about 32 times the energy per step.

left.label: Magnitude
left.text: One number for each quake: the energy released at the source, worked out from the fault's area and slip.

right.label: Shaking
right.text: Different at every place: it depends on the distance, the depth of the quake and the ground. Bedrock shakes least, soft mud most.

slides.heading: Why first estimates change
slides.text: For the quake in Panama on 9 October 2026, the first estimate was 8.0; the US Geological Survey's reviewed value is 7.7. A first estimate comes within minutes, from the stations that have recorded the quake so far. As more records arrive and the location is refined, seismologists recalculate.

slides.question: Which three things multiply together to give an earthquake's seismic moment?
options: Rock rigidity, fault area and slip
slides.explanation: Moment = rigidity × area × slip, according to the US Geological Survey. A bigger fault, or more slip, makes a bigger quake, and the magnitude is calculated from the moment.

source.label: USGS: M 7.7, 12 km WSW of Pitaloza Arriba, Panama (9 October 2026)
